rv.q: The crowd whooped along throughout this mercilessly entertaining celebration of Burton’s madcap ghost caper.

For a while, all this suffices. But gradually the thin yet complicated plot begins to stall and sag, and the spiky script, ingenious design and sheer gutsy energy of the cast aren't enough to compensate.
The script, peppered with the occasional f-word, is often genuinely witty.
The numbers are entertaining but oddly unmemorable.
All in all, there’s something surprisingly, likeably fringey about this Broadway import.
Burton’s film was a macabre joy, but this “show about death” doesn’t quite hit the mark.
The show has a lot in its favour – not least daft entertainment value – but it lacks essential spark.
It’s a classic example of what’s wrong with the West End: a haven for musical cash-ins of hit films.
This musical version, with songs by Eddie Perfect, is even less persuasive, despite some retooling of the plot in Scott Brown and Anthony King’s book.
It is, quite simply, dead good.
The real joy in the show comes from what you see, rather than what you hear.
It means the show is constantly an amusing ride, but never really flashes its teeth.
An entertaining night out, but not a memorable one.
Overall, however, it wasn’t a show that emotionally or psychologically connected with me.
But even with all the shiny packaging, Alex Timbers’ production never emotionally flies.
That said, I’m left voting "Miss" rather than "Hit", despite the best efforts of Miss Nordberg.
But rather than simply recreating the well-loved movie there's a genuine bid to translate its flimsy plot into the language of musical theatre - which makes for a breathlessly enjoyable night out.

cn.t: Critics find Beetlejuice loud, brash, and visually spectacular with impressive sets and effects, but opinions split on whether its anarchic energy compensates for a thin story and relentless pacing that prioritizes spectacle over substance.
